# Welcome

This page **runs R live in your browser** (via webR) — nothing to install. First you'll learn the core RNA-seq skills — **normalization and exploration (PCA & clustering)** — then you *adopt* a gene (it can be from **any** plant process) and characterise it through **co-expression → network → interpretation**, building a *gene dossier*. A curated **secondary-cell-wall regulatory network** is the shared case study for how *regulation* works.

**How it works**

- Edit the code where you see `______`, then press **Run** (▶). Cells share state, so run them **top to bottom**.
- Most code cells are **commented line-by-line**, so you can follow the R even if a function is new. A few Week-2 cells use pre-written **"black-box" helper functions** (e.g. betweenness, shortest paths) that you only need to *call*, not read — those are labelled as such.
- When a cell has a blank to fill, **running it prints ✅ if your answer is valid, or a hint** — no separate step.
- The heavy upstream steps (kallisto read-mapping, DESeq2) were **pre-computed** for you — this page loads the resulting tables **automatically when it opens**, so everything is instant. (A few setup cells are hidden to keep things tidy.)
- A floating **📋 Dossier** panel (bottom-left) collects your findings as you go — it **autosaves**, you can **download** it, and **"Check with AI"** gives formative feedback (no answers — it coaches). The dossier is your **assessed deliverable** for the conference.

> The expression matrix, protein-interaction edges and GO sets are **real** (Klepikova *Arabidopsis* atlas E-MTAB-7978, BioGRID, GO). The differential-expression table is a small **illustrative example** (the real one comes from the server pipeline — see the teacher guide).

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| echo: false
#| edit: false
#| output: false
# (hidden setup — runs automatically on page load)
# read.csv(path): read a comma-separated file into a data.frame (a table)
# check.names = FALSE keeps the organ column names exactly as written
m         <- read.csv("data/expression_matrix.csv", check.names = FALSE)  # genes × organ samples (TPM)
info      <- read.csv("data/gene_info.csv")        # gene_id, symbol, description
ppi       <- read.csv("data/ppi_edges.csv")        # protein–protein interactions (BioGRID)
gene_sets <- read.csv("data/gene_sets.csv")        # GO term → gene memberships
de        <- read.csv("data/de_results.csv")       # example DESeq2 result
grn       <- read.csv("data/scw_grn_edges.csv")    # curated secondary-cell-wall regulatory edges (MYB46 GRN)
connectome_grn <- read.csv("data/connectome_grn_edges.csv")  # literature GRN (PlantConnectome): directed, signed, PubMed-cited

organ_cols <- setdiff(names(m), "gene_id")          # every column except gene_id = the samples
EXPR <- as.matrix(m[, organ_cols])                  # numeric matrix (needed for cor()/apply())
rownames(EXPR) <- m$gene_id
desc <- setNames(info$description, info$gene_id)     # quick lookup: gene_id -> description
sym  <- setNames(info$symbol,      info$gene_id)
sym[is.na(sym) | sym == "nan"] <- ""                 # treat missing symbols as blank (so labels fall back to AGI)
# The curated GRN names (SND1, LAC4, NST2, ...) are authoritative for the GRN nodes, so the network
# graphs and metric tables match the case-study text and the exam answers — even where gene_info lists a
# synonym (e.g. AT1G32770 is "NAC012" in gene_info but "SND1" in the literature-curated table).
grn_syms <- c(setNames(grn$source_symbol, grn$source_AGI), setNames(grn$target_symbol, grn$target_AGI))
grn_syms <- grn_syms[!duplicated(names(grn_syms))]
grn_syms <- grn_syms[!is.na(grn_syms) & grn_syms != ""]   # never overwrite a real symbol with a blank
sym[names(grn_syms)] <- grn_syms                          # curated GRN symbols win for GRN nodes
lab <- function(a){ s <- unname(sym[a]); ifelse(is.na(s) | s == "", a, s) }   # AGI -> symbol, fall back to AGI
say  <- function(cond, good, bad)                   # tiny ✅/❌ feedback helper
  cat(if (isTRUE(cond)) paste("✅", good) else paste("❌", bad), "\n")

# draw_heatmap(): a small labelled heatmap (genes as rows, samples as columns).
# diverging = TRUE uses a blue–white–red scale centred at 0 (for z-scores).
draw_heatmap <- function(mat, main = "", diverging = FALSE){
  mat <- as.matrix(mat); ng <- nrow(mat); ns <- ncol(mat)
  if (diverging){                                    # symmetric scale around 0 (z-scores)
    pal <- hcl.colors(50, "Blue-Red 3")
    lim <- max(abs(mat), na.rm = TRUE) + 1e-9
    idx <- ceiling((mat + lim) / (2 * lim) * length(pal))
  } else {                                            # sequential scale (counts/TPM)
    pal <- hcl.colors(50, "YlGnBu", rev = TRUE)
    rng <- range(mat, na.rm = TRUE)
    idx <- ceiling((mat - rng[1]) / (diff(rng) + 1e-9) * length(pal))
  }
  idx[idx < 1] <- 1; idx[idx > length(pal)] <- length(pal)   # clamp (keeps idx a matrix)
  fmt <- function(v){                                 # compact cell label across any scale
    if (!is.finite(v)) return("")
    if (v == 0) return("0")
    if (abs(v) >= 1000) return(paste0(formatC(round(v / 1000), format = "f", digits = 0, big.mark = ","), "k"))
    if (abs(v) >= 100)  return(formatC(round(v), format = "f", digits = 0))
    formatC(signif(v, 2), format = "g")
  }
  op <- par(mar = c(5, 6, 3, 1)); on.exit(par(op))
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0.5, ns + 0.5), ylim = c(0.5, ng + 0.5),
       axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "", main = main)
  for (i in 1:ng) for (j in 1:ns){
    yy <- ng - i + 1                                 # row 1 (Gene1) drawn at the top
    cellcol <- pal[idx[i, j]]
    rect(j - 0.5, yy - 0.5, j + 0.5, yy + 0.5, col = cellcol, border = "white")
    rr <- col2rgb(cellcol)                            # readable text colour for this cell
    lum <- 0.299 * rr[1] + 0.587 * rr[2] + 0.114 * rr[3]
    text(j, yy, fmt(mat[i, j]), cex = 0.65, col = if (lum < 140) "white" else "black")
  }
  axis(1, at = 1:ns, labels = colnames(mat), las = 2, tick = FALSE, cex.axis = 0.8)
  axis(2, at = ng:1, labels = rownames(mat), las = 1, tick = FALSE, cex.axis = 0.8)
}

# draw_network(): a tiny base-R network drawer (no igraph). edges = data.frame(source, target[, type]).
# Force-directed (Fruchterman–Reingold) layout; edge colour by type; GRN edges drawn as directed arrows.
# If there are too many nodes it keeps the hub + EVERY regulatory (GRN) node, then the highest-degree rest,
# so the regulatory layer is never dropped.
draw_network <- function(edges, hub = NULL, main = "", max_nodes = 44,
                         node_col = NULL, node_cex = NULL, node_border = NULL, node_lwd = NULL){
  edges <- edges[as.character(edges$source) != as.character(edges$target), , drop = FALSE]   # no self-loops
  if (nrow(edges) == 0){ plot.new(); title(main); text(0.5, 0.5, "no edges yet"); return(invisible()) }
  edges$source <- as.character(edges$source); edges$target <- as.character(edges$target)
  etype <- if ("type" %in% names(edges)) as.character(edges$type) else rep("coexpression", nrow(edges))
  isgrn <- grepl("^GRN", etype)
  capped <- FALSE; nodes <- unique(c(edges$source, edges$target))
  if (length(nodes) > max_nodes){                              # always keep hub + all GRN nodes, then top-degree
    must <- intersect(unique(c(if (!is.null(hub)) hub, edges$source[isgrn], edges$target[isgrn])), nodes)
    deg  <- sort(table(c(edges$source, edges$target)), decreasing = TRUE)
    keep <- c(must, head(setdiff(names(deg), must), max(0, max_nodes - length(must))))
    sel  <- edges$source %in% keep & edges$target %in% keep
    edges <- edges[sel, , drop = FALSE]; etype <- etype[sel]; isgrn <- isgrn[sel]
    nodes <- unique(c(edges$source, edges$target)); capped <- TRUE
  }
  n <- length(nodes); id <- setNames(seq_len(n), nodes)
  A <- matrix(0, n, n); ai <- id[edges$source]; bi <- id[edges$target]   # undirected adjacency for layout
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(edges))){ A[ai[i], bi[i]] <- 1; A[bi[i], ai[i]] <- 1 }
  set.seed(1)                                                  # reproducible layout
  x <- cos(2*pi*(seq_len(n)-1)/n) + runif(n, -0.02, 0.02)
  y <- sin(2*pi*(seq_len(n)-1)/n) + runif(n, -0.02, 0.02)
  k <- 1/sqrt(n)
  for (it in 1:250){                                           # repel all pairs, attract along edges
    dx <- outer(x, x, "-"); dy <- outer(y, y, "-")
    d  <- sqrt(dx^2 + dy^2); d[d < 1e-3] <- 1e-3
    f  <- (k^2/d) - (d^2/k)*A
    fx <- rowSums(f * dx / d); fy <- rowSums(f * dy / d)
    fl <- sqrt(fx^2 + fy^2); fl[fl < 1e-6] <- 1e-6
    step <- 0.08*(1 - it/250) + 0.004
    x <- x + step*fx/fl; y <- y + step*fy/fl
  }
  pal_e <- c(coexpression = "grey72", PPI = "#2c7fb8", GRN_activates = "forestgreen",
             GRN_represses = "firebrick", GRN_induces = "forestgreen")
  ecol <- pal_e[etype]; ecol[is.na(ecol)] <- "grey72"
  elty <- ifelse(etype == "GRN_induces", 2, 1)
  op <- par(mar = c(1, 1, 3, 1)); on.exit(par(op))
  rng <- range(c(x, y)); pad <- 0.12*diff(rng) + 1e-6
  plot(NA, xlim = rng + c(-pad, pad), ylim = rng + c(-pad, pad), asp = 1, axes = FALSE,
       xlab = "", ylab = "", main = if (capped) paste0(main, "  (", n, " nodes shown)") else main)
  ax <- x[ai]; ay <- y[ai]; bx <- x[bi]; by <- y[bi]
  sh <- 0.045*diff(rng); ux <- bx-ax; uy <- by-ay; L <- sqrt(ux^2+uy^2); L[L < 1e-6] <- 1e-6
  for (i in which(!isgrn))                                     # co-expression / PPI as plain segments
    segments(ax[i], ay[i], bx[i], by[i], col = ecol[i], lwd = 1.5, lty = elty[i])
  for (i in which(isgrn))                                      # regulatory edges as arrows, drawn on top
    suppressWarnings(arrows(ax[i]+sh*ux[i]/L[i], ay[i]+sh*uy[i]/L[i],
                  bx[i]-sh*ux[i]/L[i], by[i]-sh*uy[i]/L[i],
                  length = 0.08, lwd = 2.6, col = ecol[i], lty = elty[i]))
  ishub <- if (is.null(hub)) rep(FALSE, n) else nodes == hub
  fillv <- if (!is.null(node_col))    node_col[nodes]    else ifelse(ishub, "gold", "white")
  cexv  <- if (!is.null(node_cex))    node_cex[nodes]    else ifelse(ishub, 3.4, 2.3)
  bordv <- if (!is.null(node_border)) node_border[nodes] else rep("grey25", n)
  lwdv  <- if (!is.null(node_lwd))    node_lwd[nodes]    else rep(1.4, n)
  fillv[is.na(fillv)] <- "white"; bordv[is.na(bordv)] <- "grey25"
  cexv[is.na(cexv)] <- 2.3; lwdv[is.na(lwdv)] <- 1.4
  points(x, y, pch = 21, cex = cexv, bg = fillv, col = bordv, lwd = lwdv)
  labs <- sym[nodes]; bad <- is.na(labs) | labs == ""; labs[bad] <- nodes[bad]
  text(x, y, labs, cex = 0.62, font = ifelse(ishub, 2, 1))
  present <- intersect(c("coexpression","PPI","GRN_activates","GRN_represses","GRN_induces"), etype)
  legend("topright", bty = "n", cex = 0.72, legend = present, col = pal_e[present],
         lwd = 2, lty = ifelse(present == "GRN_induces", 2, 1))
}

# cynet(): emit a network as a text marker that cynet.html turns into an INTERACTIVE cytoscape.js
# graph (drag / zoom / pan) showing the network you just built.
cynet <- function(edges, hub = NULL, id = "cy", title = "",
                  node_fill = NULL, node_size = NULL, node_border = NULL, node_lwd = NULL){
  edges <- edges[as.character(edges$source) != as.character(edges$target), , drop = FALSE]
  if (nrow(edges) == 0){ cat("(no edges to draw yet)\n"); return(invisible(NULL)) }
  src <- as.character(edges$source); tgt <- as.character(edges$target)
  ty  <- if ("type" %in% names(edges)) as.character(edges$type) else rep("coexpression", length(src))
  nodes <- unique(c(src, tgt)); grn_src <- unique(src[grepl("^GRN", ty)])
  clean <- function(s){ s <- gsub('[\\\\"]', '', s); gsub('@@', '', s) }     # keep JSON + marker safe
  lab <- sym[nodes]; lab[is.na(lab) | lab == ""] <- nodes[is.na(lab) | lab == ""]
  hubv <- if (is.null(hub)) rep(FALSE, length(nodes)) else nodes == hub
  pick <- function(v, d){ if (is.null(v)) return(rep(d, length(nodes))); x <- v[nodes]; x[is.na(x)] <- d; x }
  fillv <- pick(node_fill, ""); sizev <- pick(node_size, 0)
  bordv <- pick(node_border, ""); lwdv <- pick(node_lwd, 0)
  nj <- paste0('{"id":"', nodes, '","label":"', clean(lab),
               '","hub":', tolower(as.character(hubv)),
               ',"reg":', tolower(as.character(nodes %in% grn_src)),
               ',"col":"', fillv, '","sz":', sizev, ',"bc":"', bordv, '","bw":', lwdv, '}', collapse = ",")
  ej <- paste0('{"s":"', src, '","t":"', tgt, '","ty":"', ty, '"}', collapse = ",")
  cat("\n@@CYNET@@", '{"id":"', id, '","title":"', clean(title),
      '","nodes":[', nj, '],"edges":[', ej, ']}', "@@END@@\n", sep = "")
  invisible(NULL)
}

cat(sprintf("✅ Data loaded: %d genes × %d organ samples. You're ready.\n",
            nrow(EXPR), length(organ_cols)))
```

# Week 1 — uge 43 · clean data → what does my gene do?

## 📅 Tuesday 21 Oct · 09:00–12:00 {.dayband}

::: {.dayband-sub}
Today you do **M4.W1.E1** only — normalization.
:::

### M4.W1.E1 — Normalization: raw counts → TPM → log → z-score

This stage builds the standard normalization pipeline one metric at a time, and shows the matrix as a heatmap after each step so you can *see* what every transformation fixes. The aim is for you to understand **why** each metric exists, not just how to type it.

kallisto gives you **estimated counts** per gene. You **cannot compare counts directly** — two things confound them that have nothing to do with biology:

- **gene length** — a longer gene catches more reads even at the same expression level;
- **sequencing depth** — a sample sequenced deeper has more reads *everywhere*.

**TPM** (Transcripts Per Million) removes both: divide out length, then scale each sample to a million. We then **log-transform** (to tame the huge dynamic range) and **z-score** (to compare each gene's *pattern* across samples). The *Arabidopsis* atlas you analyse in the next stages is already in TPM — here you'll see exactly where it comes from. But first: **always look at the raw data.**

```{webr}
genes   <- paste0("Gene", 1:12)
samples <- c("Root1","Root2","Root3","Leaf1","Leaf2","Leaf3","Pollen1")
# ONE table to play with: the 7 sample counts + each gene's length (bp) in the last column.
# matrix(values, byrow = TRUE) fills it row by row. Change any number and re-run — nothing else needs editing.
mat <- matrix(c(
#  Root1  Root2 Root3 Leaf1 Leaf2 Leaf3 Pollen1   length
   80,    85,   78,   2,    1,    3,    0,        1500,
   90,   100,   88,   5,    2,    4,    0,        2400,
    2,     1,    3,  70,   75,   80,    0,         900,
    3,     2,    4,  85,   82,   90,    0,        3000,
    0,     1,    0,   2,    1,    0,  120,         600,
   20,    20,   20,  20,   20,   20,   20,        1200,
    0,     0,    1,   0,    0,    0,    0,        1800,
    5,100000,    6,   7,    5,    6,    8,         300,
   10,    15,   12,  25,   30,   28,    5,        2100,
   40,    38,   42,  45,   47,   50,   41,        4500,
    5,     9,    6,  12,   15,   11,    4,         750,
    3,     5,    4,  30,   28,   26,   10,        1350),
  nrow = 12, byrow = TRUE, dimnames = list(genes, c(samples, "length")))

mat[, "Root1"] <- mat[, "Root1"] * 100   # simulate Root1 sequenced ~100x deeper (a whole-sample depth artefact)

counts   <- mat[, samples]               # the count matrix (genes x samples) — what we analyse and plot
gene_len <- mat[, "length"]              # each gene's length (bp), read straight from the table above

draw_heatmap(counts, "Raw counts")       # labelled heatmap (helper is pre-defined for you)
```

> **Look closely:** can you see any tissue pattern? You can't — **one cell, `Gene8` in `Root2` = 100000, swamps the entire colour scale.** That single spike is almost certainly a **technical artifact** — and it's exactly why you must *eyeball* the raw matrix before trusting any analysis. Furthermore, **`Root1` (the first column) has far more reads than the other samples** — another technical artefact, this time caused by **deeper sequencing** of that one library.

#### Step 1.1 — Find the outlier

The aim here is to **locate the single most extreme value** and name the gene and sample it belongs to — one artefactual cell can quietly distort every mean, total and correlation you compute later. This also teaches **matrix indexing**: in R you read a matrix as `counts[row, column]`.

**Replace the `______`** in the cell below with the correct column number (look at the heatmap above), then press **Run** — the ✅/❌ line tells you whether you found the outlier.

```{webr}
# In R a matrix is indexed counts[row, column]:
#   ROWS    are the genes   (row 1 = Gene1, ..., row 12 = Gene12)
#   COLUMNS are the samples (column 1 = Root1, column 2 = Root2, ..., column 7 = Pollen1)
biggest <- max(counts)                    # the largest value anywhere in the matrix

# From the heatmap, the spike sits in the Root2 column. Enter that COLUMN number:
col_num <- ______                         # <- blank: 2   (Root2 is the 2nd column)

# now find which ROW (gene) holds that maximum within the chosen column
row_num <- which(counts[, col_num] == biggest)
gene    <- rownames(counts)[row_num]      # row number  -> gene name
sample  <- colnames(counts)[col_num]      # column number -> sample name
cat("counts[", row_num, ",", col_num, "] =", counts[row_num, col_num], "->", gene, "in", sample, "\n")

say(length(row_num) == 1 && sample == "Root2" && gene == "Gene8",
    "correct — counts[8, 2] = Gene8 in Root2 is the outlier (a spike that also inflates that whole sample).",
    "the spike is in the 2nd column (Root2) — set col_num <- 2 and re-run.")
```

#### Step 1.2 — Why raw counts aren't comparable

The aim of this step is to make the two confounds concrete *before* we correct them, so the normalization that follows feels motivated rather than magical. We print the per-sample read totals (sequencing depth) and the per-gene lengths — two technical factors that change counts without any change in real expression. **Run this** to see both in your toy data:

```{webr}
# 1) sequencing depth = total reads per sample (the sum of each column)
depth <- colSums(counts)
cat("── Sequencing depth: total reads per sample ──\n")
print(data.frame(sample = names(depth), total_reads = as.integer(depth), row.names = NULL))

# 2) gene length in base pairs (one value per gene)
cat("\n── Gene length (bp): longer genes collect more reads ──\n")
print(data.frame(gene = names(gene_len), length_bp = gene_len, row.names = NULL))
```

> Look at the totals: **`Root2` (~100,000 reads) and `Root1` (~26,000) dwarf the others (~300).** `Root1` was simply sequenced deeper; `Root2`'s total is almost entirely the `Gene8` artefact — and a single count that large is itself only possible in a deeply-sequenced library, so `Root2` is deep *too*. Both totals are **technical, not biological**. And gene-wise, **`Gene12` (1350 bp) collects more reads than `Gene11` (750 bp) at the *same* expression**, simply because it is longer. TPM fixes **both kinds** — length first, then depth.

#### Step 1.3 — Compute TPM (length, then depth)

The aim is to remove the two confounds from Step 1.2 and end with **TPM**, the metric the atlas uses. TPM is two normalizations done **in order** — do them one at a time, each with its own check.

**Step 1.3a — divide out gene length (→ RPK).** **RPK = Reads Per Kilobase**: the read count divided by the gene's length in **kilobases** (1 kb = 1000 bp). After this step a long gene and a short gene at the same true expression give the same number. Fill the blank, then **Run**.

```{webr}
# gene_len is in bp, so /1000 converts it to kilobases. gene_len has one value per gene (per row),
# so it lines up with the matrix rows automatically.
rpk <- counts / (gene_len / ______)            # <- blank: 1000   (bp -> kb)

draw_heatmap(counts, "Raw counts — length & depth still in")
draw_heatmap(rpk,    "After step 1 (RPK) — gene length removed")

say(exists("rpk") && all(is.finite(rpk)),
    "RPK done — values are now per-kilobase, so a long gene and a short gene at the same true expression read alike.",
    "the blank is 1000 (bp -> kb): rpk <- counts / (gene_len / 1000).")
```

**Step 1.3b — divide out sequencing depth (→ TPM).** Now scale each *sample* so its values sum to **1,000,000**. Each sample's own total is `colSums(rpk)`. Fill the blank, then **Run**.

```{webr}
# sweep(x, 2, v, "/") divides each COLUMN by the matching value in v; * 1e6 scales to per-million.
tpm <- sweep(rpk, 2, ______, "/") * 1e6        # <- blank: colSums(rpk)

draw_heatmap(tpm, "After step 2 (TPM) — depth removed too (raw scale)")

say(exists("tpm") && all(abs(colSums(tpm) - 1e6) < 1),
    "that's TPM — every sample sums to 1,000,000 and gene length is divided out. This is exactly the form the atlas is in.",
    "the blank is colSums(rpk): each sample is divided by its own RPK total, then x 1e6.")
```

<details><summary>💡 Hint</summary>
RPK = counts ÷ (length in kb). Then for each sample, divide by that sample's own RPK total (<code>colSums(rpk)</code>) and multiply by 1,000,000.
</details>

> Look carefully at the TPM heatmap: you can **just** start to make out **Leaf1–Leaf3 sharing a pattern**, and **Root1 & Root3** sharing another — but **Root2 still looks odd**, because the `Gene8` artefact dominates it (normalization does **not** remove outliers). It's still hard to read, since a few large values dominate the colour scale — which is exactly why we next **log-transform** (Step 1.4) and then **z-score** (Step 1.5).

#### Step 1.4 — Log scaling

The aim is to make a matrix that spans several orders of magnitude actually *readable*. Taking **log2(TPM + 1)** compresses the range — every doubling becomes one even step — so moderate and low-expressed genes stop being invisible next to the high ones; the `+ 1` keeps zeros finite (log2(0 + 1) = 0). **Fill the blank with `tpm`** (the matrix from Step 1.3), then Run and compare with the TPM heatmap above.

```{webr}
log_tpm <- log2(______ + 1)              # <- blank: tpm   (+1 so a zero stays finite: log2(0+1)=0)
draw_heatmap(log_tpm, "log2(TPM + 1)")

say(exists("log_tpm") && all(is.finite(log_tpm)),
    "log scale: the dynamic range is tamed, so the root / leaf / pollen patterns start to show.",
    "fill the blank with tpm (the matrix from Step 1.3), then re-run.")
```

#### Step 1.5 — Z-score (compare each gene's pattern)

The aim is to compare each gene's *pattern* across samples, not its absolute level. A **z-score per gene** — subtract that gene's mean and divide by its standard deviation across samples — recentres every gene on 0, so the heatmap shows where each gene is relatively high (red) or low (blue) regardless of how strongly it is expressed. This is the standard transform behind clustering heatmaps, and here it makes the tissue specificity jump out.

```{webr}
# z-score each GENE (row): subtract that gene's own mean, divide by its own SD across samples.
# Subtracting a length-12 vector from the matrix recycles DOWN the rows, so each gene gets its own mean.
row_mean <- rowMeans(log_tpm)            # each gene's mean across the 7 samples
row_sd   <- apply(log_tpm, 1, sd)        # each gene's standard deviation
z <- (______ - row_mean) / row_sd        # <- blank: log_tpm   (subtract each gene's mean, divide by its SD)
z[!is.finite(z)] <- 0                    # a gene with no variation would divide by 0 -> set to 0
draw_heatmap(z, "Per-gene z-score of log2(TPM)", diverging = TRUE)

say(exists("z") && abs(mean(z)) < 1e-6,
    "z-scored: each gene now centres on 0 — Gene1–2 root-high, Gene3–4 leaf-high, Gene5 pollen-specific stand out clearly. But Root2 still looks off (see below).",
    "the blank is log_tpm:  z <- (log_tpm - row_mean) / row_sd.")
```

> **But look at `Root2`.** Even after z-scoring, `Root2` still doesn't line up with `Root1`/`Root3` — its whole column looks scrambled. That's `Gene8` *still* making trouble: because TPM forces every sample to sum to a million, the `Gene8` spike ate most of `Root2`'s budget and deflated every *other* gene in that sample (Step 1.3). A per-gene z-score recentres each gene on its own mean, but it **cannot** undo a distortion that lives in one entire *column* — so z-scoring did **not** rescue `Root2`. The only fix is to remove `Gene8` and re-normalize, which is exactly what M4.W1.E2 does next.
>
> **Rule for your dossier:** *estimated counts → differential expression; TPM → comparing a gene across samples; log / z-score → visualising and clustering.*

## 📅 Thursday 23 Oct · 09:00–16:00 {.dayband}

::: {.dayband-sub}
Today you do **M4.W1.E2 → M4.W1.E5** — PCA & clustering, claim your gene, co-expression, then the databases.
:::

### M4.W1.E2 — Explore the structure: PCA & clustering

Now that the matrix is normalized, step back and ask whether the **samples** group the way biology predicts — and deal with the `Gene8` artefact honestly. We do it in the right order: **first see the damage** the artefact does to the global picture, **then** remove it and re-normalize, and watch the structure snap into place. *(Run M4.W1.E1 first so `counts`, `gene_len` and `z` exist.)*

#### PCA — first, with the artefact still in

PCA squeezes the genes into a few **principal components** that capture the most variation between samples; if normalization worked, samples should separate by **tissue**. Let's run it first on the matrix **from Step 1.5 — `Gene8` still included** — and see what one bad gene does.

```{webr}
# z is the per-gene z-score from Step 1.5 — it STILL contains Gene8.
tissue <- c("Root","Root","Root","Leaf","Leaf","Leaf","Pollen")   # label each sample
pca0 <- prcomp(t(z))                                              # PCA with samples as rows
op <- par(mar = c(4, 4, 3, 7))                                    # extra right margin for the legend
plot(pca0$x[,1], pca0$x[,2], col = factor(tissue), pch = 19, cex = 1.6,
     xlab = "PC1", ylab = "PC2", main = "PCA — Gene8 (artefact) still in")
text(pca0$x[,1], pca0$x[,2], colnames(z), pos = 3, cex = 0.7)
legend(par("usr")[2] * 1.02, par("usr")[4], xpd = TRUE, bty = "n",
       legend = levels(factor(tissue)), col = 1:3, pch = 19)
par(op)
```

> **What goes wrong.** `Root2` is dragged away from `Root1`/`Root3` — the three roots **don't** group. The `Gene8` spike, even after per-gene z-scoring, distorts `Root2`'s whole profile (TPM's sum-to-million crushed every other gene in that sample, Step 1.5). One bad gene is enough to break the global picture.

#### Remove the artefact and re-normalize

Sometimes a gene — or even a whole sample — is so badly behaved that **no normalization can rescue it**; you detect it, document *why*, and remove it. `Gene8` is exactly such a case. We drop it and re-run the **same** TPM → log → z-score pipeline on the clean matrix.

```{webr}
# Gene8 was the artefact (Step 1.1). Drop it, then re-run the SAME pipeline — this is the compact,
# "pro" way an analyst writes the whole TPM -> log -> z-score in a few lines:
keep <- rownames(counts) != "Gene8"
crpk <- counts[keep, ] / (gene_len[keep] / 1000)          # TPM step 1: divide out gene length
ctpm <- sweep(crpk, 2, colSums(crpk), "/") * 1e6          # TPM step 2: divide out depth
clog <- log2(ctpm + 1)                                    # log
cz   <- (clog - rowMeans(clog)) / apply(clog, 1, sd)      # per-gene z-score (same row trick as Step 1.5)
cz[!is.finite(cz)] <- 0
tissue <- c("Root","Root","Root","Leaf","Leaf","Leaf","Pollen")   # label each sample
cat("Clean, re-normalized matrix:", nrow(cz), "genes ×", ncol(cz), "samples\n")
draw_heatmap(cz, "Per-gene z-score of log2(TPM) — Gene8 removed", diverging = TRUE)
```

> With the artefact gone, the z-score heatmap already shows clean tissue blocks — root genes high (red) in the root samples, leaf genes high in the leaves, and so on.
>
> **🔬 Task:** change the first line to **keep** Gene8 — e.g. `keep <- rownames(counts) != "none"` — re-run this cell, the PCA below, *and* the clustering. Watch `Root2` break away again. That's *why* you remove artefacts before analysis.

#### PCA — after removing the artefact

Now the same PCA on the **clean** matrix `cz`. The three tissues should fall into three tight groups.

```{webr}
# prcomp(t(cz)): PCA with SAMPLES as rows (t() transposes). cz is already z-scored per gene.
pca <- prcomp(t(cz))
op <- par(mar = c(4, 4, 3, 7))                                 # extra right margin for the legend
# pca$x = sample coordinates; [,1]/[,2] are PC1/PC2.  factor(tissue): turn labels into colour groups
plot(pca$x[,1], pca$x[,2], col = factor(tissue), pch = 19, cex = 1.6,
     xlab = "PC1", ylab = "PC2", main = "PCA of samples — Gene8 removed")
text(pca$x[,1], pca$x[,2], colnames(cz), pos = 3, cex = 0.7)   # text(): label each point
legend(par("usr")[2] * 1.02, par("usr")[4], xpd = TRUE, bty = "n",   # just OUTSIDE the plot, top-right
       legend = levels(factor(tissue)), col = 1:3, pch = 19)
par(op)
```

> Compare with the first PCA: removing one gene and re-normalizing pulled `Root2` back in with the other roots. **That** is the payoff of `detect → remove → re-normalize`.

How much of the variation does each component capture? The **scree plot** answers that — and tells you whether the 2-D PCA picture can be trusted.

```{webr}
# pca$sdev = standard deviation of each PC; squared = variance. Divide by the total for a proportion.
var_explained <- pca$sdev^2 / sum(pca$sdev^2)
barplot(100 * var_explained, names.arg = paste0("PC", seq_along(var_explained)),
        ylab = "% variance explained", main = "Scree plot")
cat(sprintf("PC1 captures %.0f%% of the variance, PC2 %.0f%% — together %.0f%%.\n",
            100*var_explained[1], 100*var_explained[2], 100*sum(var_explained[1:2])))
```

> **What it means:** each bar is the share of total variation that component captures. Here a couple of tall bars (PC1–PC2) hold most of it, so the data is essentially **low-dimensional** and the 2-D PCA plot above is a *faithful* summary of the samples. If instead the bars were all roughly equal height, no 2-D plot could represent the data and you should distrust any clustering you read off it.

#### Hierarchical clustering — which samples are most alike?

Clustering repeatedly joins the two most similar samples into a tree (a **dendrogram**); samples from the same tissue should join first. We measure similarity as the distance between samples in z-score space. The **linkage** is the rule for *how* clusters merge — and it changes the tree.

```{webr}
LINK <- "ward.D2"            # <- try also: "complete", "average", "single" — then re-run
d  <- dist(t(cz))            # dist(): pairwise distances between samples (rows of t(cz))
hc <- hclust(d, method = LINK)
plot(hc, labels = colnames(cz), main = paste("Clustering of samples —", LINK, "linkage"), xlab = "", sub = "")
```

> **🔬 Explore the linkage.** Re-run with `LINK <- "single"`, then `"complete"`, then `"average"`. **Single** linkage often *chains* samples into one straggly cluster (it joins on the single closest pair); **complete** and **ward.D2** give compact, balanced clusters — which is why ward.D2 is a common default. Note under each method whether the three tissues still separate, and whether `Root2` joins the roots or hangs off on its own.

**🔮 Your turn:** there are **three** tissues here, so cut the tree into three groups and check they match. **Fill the blank** with `3`, then **Run**.

```{webr}
# cutree(hc, k): cut the dendrogram into k groups (k = number of tissues here)
groups <- cutree(hc, k = ______)        # <- blank: 3   (root, leaf, pollen)

# colour each LEAF LABEL by its cluster, so you can read the cut straight off the tree
pal3 <- c("forestgreen", "firebrick", "steelblue", "orange")   # one colour per cluster
dend <- as.dendrogram(hc)
dend <- dendrapply(dend, function(node){
  if (is.leaf(node)) {                                  # only the tips carry sample names
    s <- attr(node, "label")                            # the sample at this leaf
    attr(node, "nodePar") <- list(lab.col = pal3[groups[s]], pch = NA)
  }
  node
})
plot(dend, main = "Samples coloured by cluster", ylab = "Height")
print(data.frame(sample = colnames(cz), tissue = tissue, cluster = groups))

say(exists("groups") && length(unique(groups)) == 3,
    "three clusters that line up with root / leaf / pollen — once the artefact is removed, the structure is purely biological.",
    "we have three tissues, so cut the tree into 3 groups.")
```

> Notice this only worked **after** removing `Gene8`: with the artefact in, its spike dominated `Root2` and scrambled the clustering — no choice of linkage fixes that, you have to remove the bad data.

### M4.W1.E3 — Claim your gene

You've got the skills — now make it personal. Pick **one** gene — your TA spreads them so every group gets a **different biology**. These span very different processes; your job is to *discover* what yours does and where it acts.

**Secondary cell wall** *(the Week-2 network case study)*:

- `CESA7 AT5G17420` — cellulose synthase
- `IRX9 AT2G37090` — xylan biosynthesis
- `LAC4 AT2G38080` — laccase (lignin)
- `MYB46 AT5G12870` — master TF (the GRN hub)

**Other processes** *(each a different module)*:

- `CAB1 AT1G29930` — photosynthesis
- `AP3 AT3G54340` — flower (B-class organ identity; co-expresses with its partner **PI** — try cutoff ~0.80)
- `OLE1 AT4G25140` — seed oil-body
- `NCED3 AT3G14440` — abiotic stress / ABA (rate-limiting drought-response enzyme)
- `PR1 AT2G14610` — pathogen defence
- `SAG13 AT2G29350` — senescence
- `HTA6 AT5G59870` — histone H2A (cell cycle / DNA replication)
- `TT4 AT5G13930` — flavonoid / anthocyanin biosynthesis

**Ribosomal proteins — two compartments** *(a built-in comparison)*:

- `RPL19A AT1G02780` — cytosolic (translation)
- `RPL15 AT3G25920` — plastid / chloroplast

*In this developmental atlas the **cytosolic** ribosome tracks the cell's growth / translation programme, while the **plastid** ribosome tracks **photosynthesis** (chloroplast biogenesis) — adopt both to see the split. (The **mitochondrial** ribosome co-varies with the cytosolic one, so it isn't a separate module here — and ribosomal genes have little documented regulation, so their **N3 layer is often empty**: a real "housekeeping" finding.)*

**Instructions:** replace the `______` with your gene's AGI code, then **Run** — the cell tells you if your gene is valid.

```{webr}
MY_GENE <- "______"        # <- the AGI locus CODE, e.g. "AT5G17420"  (must be exact - this is what looks the gene up)
MY_NAME <- lab(MY_GENE)    # the gene's symbol, looked up for you (falls back to the AGI if it has none)
cat("Adopted:", MY_NAME, "(", MY_GENE, ")\n")   # cat() prints its arguments

# instant check: grepl() tests the AGI text pattern; %in% checks the gene is actually in the data
say(grepl("^AT[1-5CM]G[0-9]{5}$", MY_GENE) && MY_GENE %in% rownames(EXPR),
    "valid gene, present in the data — onwards!",
    "not a valid/known locus — pick one from the pool above and re-run.")
```

<details><summary>💡 Hint</summary>
An AGI locus looks like `AT` + chromosome (1–5) + `G` + five digits, in quotes: `"AT5G17420"`.
</details>

**✍️ Dossier:** write your hypothesis — *genes co-expressed with my gene are enriched for ______, so my gene acts in ______.* *(Open the **📋 Dossier** panel, bottom-left, and fill the "Hypothesis" field — it autosaves and an AI tutor can check it.)*

### M4.W1.E4 — Co-expression: find your gene's neighbours

Before you reach for a database or build a network, do the simplest, most powerful trick in transcriptomics yourself: **guilt by association**. Genes that rise and fall *together* across many samples are often part of the same process — so the genes whose expression profile most resembles your gene's are your first, data-driven guess at what it does.

We measure "resembles" with the **Pearson correlation** of each gene's profile against your gene's, then sort: the top of the list is your gene's **co-expression neighbourhood**. *(Run M4.W1.E3 first so `MY_GENE` is set.)*

```{webr}
HUB    <- MY_GENE                                  # your adopted gene (from M4.W1.E3)
target <- EXPR[HUB, ]                              # its expression across every organ
# cor(r, target): Pearson correlation of each gene's profile with your gene's profile
pcc  <- apply(EXPR, 1, function(r) suppressWarnings(cor(r, ______)))   # <- blank: target
nbhd <- data.frame(gene = rownames(EXPR), symbol = lab(rownames(EXPR)),
                   description = substr(desc[rownames(EXPR)], 1, 40), PCC = round(pcc, 3),
                   row.names = NULL)               # row.names = NULL -> the AGI appears ONCE, in the gene column
nbhd <- head(nbhd[order(-nbhd$PCC), ], 60)         # keep the top-60 neighbours
print(head(nbhd, 12), right = FALSE, row.names = FALSE)   # left-aligned: gene | symbol | description | PCC

say(nrow(nbhd) > 0 && nbhd$gene[1] == HUB && round(nbhd$PCC[1], 3) == 1,
    paste("row 1 is", MY_NAME, "at PCC = 1.000 — neighbour list ready."),
    "row 1 should be your own gene at PCC = 1.000 — fill the blank with 'target' and re-run.")
```

**🤔 Read your neighbourhood — why does *your own gene* sit at the very top of its list, at PCC = 1.000?**

<details><summary>💡 Hint</summary>A gene's expression profile is identical to itself, and the Pearson correlation of any profile with itself is exactly 1.0 — so every gene is its own perfect "neighbour". (It's also a quick sanity check that the correlation ran correctly.)</details>

> Now look at rows 2–12: do they form **one biological programme**? For a wall gene you'll see a tight secondary-cell-wall module — other `CESA`s, laccases, xylan / `FLA` / `IRX` genes. **For another process** the module is different but just as tight: a *photosynthesis* gene pulls in `LHCB`/photosystem genes, a *histone* pulls in other histones + `PCNA` (DNA replication), a *ribosomal* protein pulls in other `RPL`/`RPS` genes (translation), a *defence* gene pulls in pathogen-response genes. **Your job is to name the one process those neighbours share** — "these are mostly photosynthesis genes", "these are mostly ribosomal proteins", "these are mostly cell-wall genes". That short label *is* your gene's predicted function, and it goes straight into your dossier. You do **not** need to recognise every gene in the list — recognising a handful is enough to name the module.

**🤔 Look at the PCC of your top neighbour (row 2) — it will be high. Does a high correlation *prove* that the two proteins interact, or that one regulates the other?**

<details><summary>💡 Hint</summary>No — a high correlation only means the two genes share an expression <i>pattern</i>. That is <i>consistent with</i> a functional link, but it could equally come from both being switched on by the same upstream regulator, or both being specific to the same tissue. Proof needs <b>physical</b> (PPI) or <b>directed</b> (regulatory) evidence — which you add in <b>Week 2</b>, where you turn this ranked list into a real network and see where co-expression does and doesn't line up with mechanism.</details>

> **✍️ Dossier:** record your **top 5 co-expressed genes** (symbol + PCC) and, in one line, the process they suggest your gene acts in. *(Open the **📋 Dossier** panel, bottom-left, and fill the "Co-expression" field.)*

### M4.W1.E5 · Database exercises — the database half of your dossier (D1–D3)

Every number so far came from **one** atlas. Real evidence is a *consensus* across resources. In these three short **web** exercises (no coding — just clicking) you cross-examine **your adopted gene** in the major plant databases and fill **one results table**: the database half of your gene dossier. Each step puts the co-expression list you built in **M4.W1.E4** to the test — you stay on **your own gene** the whole way through, and you carry it into Week 2.

**📋 Your database dossier — the 6 things to record.** Work down this list as you do D1 → D3 and write your answers in the **📋 Dossier panel** (bottom-left of this page) or on paper. The last column shows what a *complete* answer looks like, using **CESA7** as the worked example — your gene will have different answers, but the same shape. *(This is the database part of your dossier — 20% of the grade.)*

| # | What to record | Where to get it | Example — if your gene were **CESA7** |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Protein domain (Pfam) | **D1** → PEO | cellulose synthase (`Cellulose_synt`) |
| 2 | Highest-expressing organ | **D1** → ePlant *(re-checked in D3)* | mature / inflorescence stem |
| 3 | Highest cell type / tissue (finer than the organ) | **D1** → ePlant *(Root eFP or another tissue view)* | root xylem |
| 4 | Top 3 co-expressed genes (databases) | **D2** → CoNekT | CESA4, CESA8, FLA11 |
| 5 | Does the top organ agree across all 3 databases? | **D3** | yes |
| 6 | **Your one-line function + the evidence for it** | synthesis of 1–5 | *"Secondary-wall cellulose synthase — stem/xylem expression (eFP+PEO+EBI), CESA4/CESA8 co-expression reproduced in CoNekT, and a cellulose-synthase Pfam domain."* |

#### D1 — What is my gene, and where is it on?  *(ePlant eFP + PEO)*

1. **ePlant** ([bar.utoronto.ca/eplant](https://bar.utoronto.ca/eplant/)) → search your gene (e.g. `AT5G17420` CESA7, `AT5G12870` MYB46) → **Plant eFP**: record the **highest organ** + colour scale.
2. Now go finer than the organ: open the **cell-type / tissue-level views** (e.g. **Tissue-Specific Root eFP**) and record the **highest-expressing cell type or tissue** you can find for your gene. *(A secondary-cell-wall gene lights up the root **xylem**, where thick lignified walls are built; a photosynthesis gene the leaf mesophyll; a seed gene the embryo or endosperm. If your gene is simply **not expressed in root**, that is a real result — record its top tissue from the Plant eFP instead and say so.)*
3. **PEO** ([peo.ku.dk](https://peo.ku.dk/)) → same locus → record **(a)** highest organ (agrees with ePlant?); **(b)** the **top 3 co-expressed genes** (how many SCW genes do you already recognise — other `CESA`s, `IRX9`, `COBL4`, `KNAT7`, `MYB46/83`?); **(c)** the **protein domain** (Pfam) — the annotation skills from the database & sequence modules.

> ✅ *Expected:* a wall gene peaks in **inflorescence/mature stem** and localises to root **xylem**; its PEO co-expressed list is full of SCW genes and the domain matches the family (cellulose-synthase for a CESA, MYB DNA-binding for MYB46, laccase for LAC4). **Other genes tell their own consistent story** — e.g. CAB1 peaks in *leaves* with *photosynthesis* neighbours; a histone peaks in dividing tissue with other histones; a ribosomal protein with the translation module. Whatever your gene, the databases should *agree* on its tissue, partners and domain.
> **→ Dossier:** Pfam domain · highest organ · highest cell type / tissue · top 3 co-expressed.

#### D2 — Who does my gene work with?  *(CoNekT)*

1. **CoNekT** ([conekt.ku.dk](https://conekt.ku.dk/)) → search your gene → open its **co-expression neighbourhood** and click **View neighbourhood as graph**. Write down the neighbours you recognise and the **process they point to**.
2. Record your **top 3 co-expressed genes** from that graph.

> ✅ *Expected:* CoNekT returns a tight module pointing at a single process — for a wall gene other wall genes, for a photosynthesis gene the light-harvesting set, for a ribosomal protein other ribosomal proteins. CoNekT is built from a **different** set of experiments than our atlas, so if it names the same process your M4.W1.E4 list did, that agreement is real evidence.
> **→ Dossier:** top 3 co-expressed genes from CoNekT.

#### D3 — Cross-database consistency  *(PEO + EBI Expression Atlas + CoNekT)*

1. **PEO** ([peo.ku.dk](https://peo.ku.dk/)) → your gene → top organ.
2. **EBI Expression Atlas** → `ebi.ac.uk/gxa/genes/<your AGI>` (e.g. [ebi.ac.uk/gxa/genes/AT5G17420](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/gxa/genes/AT5G17420)) → Baseline → top tissue.
3. **CoNekT** → your gene → specificity → top organ.
4. Fill a 3-row table: *database | top organ | agrees?*

> ✅ *Expected:* all three converge on **stem**; the second-ranked organs may differ.
> **→ Dossier:** "top organ — agrees across 3 DBs? yes / no".

### 📝 Week 1 — exam-style questions  *(assessed; 2025-exam style, point-scored)*

Close the week the way the exam tests it — these cover **all of Week 1**: **M4.W1.E1–E4** **and** the database exercises (**E5**). Answer in 2–4 sentences; the model answers and their points match the grading. **(8 questions · 31 p.)**

#### Data, normalization & exploration (M4.W1.E1–E2)

**Q1 (4 p) — Why normalize.** Raw counts can't be compared (a) between two *genes* in one sample, nor (b) for one *gene* between two samples. Give the confound in each case and the TPM step that removes it.

<details><summary>✅ Model answer (4 p)</summary>(a) <b>Gene length</b> — a longer gene collects more reads at equal expression; divide each count by gene length in kb (the RPK step) (2 p). (b) <b>Sequencing depth</b> — samples differ in total reads; scale each sample so its values sum to 1,000,000 (the per-million step) (2 p).</details>

**Q2 (4 p) — The artefact normalization can't fix.** One gene (`Gene8`) had a huge count in `Root2`. (a) Why did TPM fail to remove the distortion — and even push the *other* genes in `Root2` down? (b) How did PCA reveal it, and why did removing the gene + re-normalizing repair the clustering?

<details><summary>✅ Model answer (4 p)</summary>(a) TPM forces every sample to sum to 1e6, so one runaway gene eats most of `Root2`'s budget and <b>deflates every other gene</b> in that column — a composition effect scaling cannot undo (2 p). (b) In PCA `Root2` separated from the other roots; dropping `Gene8` and re-normalizing restored each sample's true composition, so samples clustered by tissue (2 p).</details>

**Q3 (4 p) — z-score & clustering.** (a) Why z-score each gene before clustering samples? (b) Your clustering only separated root/leaf/pollen *after* `Gene8` was removed. Why could no choice of linkage or distance fix it while the artefact was still in?

<details><summary>✅ Model answer (4 p)</summary>(a) Per-gene z-scoring compares each gene's <b>pattern</b>, not its magnitude, so highly expressed genes don't dominate the distance and weakly expressed but informative genes still count (2 p). (b) The artefact was one enormous value that dominated every distance involving <b>Root2</b>. Clustering can only re-arrange the distances it is given, so corrupted data has to be <b>removed</b> — normalization rescales values, it cannot undo a bad measurement (2 p).</details>

**Q4 (4 p) — PCA & the scree plot.** Your scree plot shows PC1 = 62 %, PC2 = 21 %. (a) What does each bar mean, and can you trust the 2-D PCA picture here? (b) What would it mean if all the bars were roughly equal height? (c) *Before* you removed Gene8, why did Root2 sit apart on PC1?

<details><summary>✅ Model answer (4 p)</summary>(a) Each bar = the share of total variance that component captures; PC1 + PC2 = 83 %, so the 2-D plot is a <b>faithful</b> summary — most structure lives in two dimensions (2 p). (b) Variance spread evenly across many PCs → the data is genuinely high-dimensional, no 2-D plot represents it, and you should distrust any clustering read off it (1 p). (c) The Gene8 spike — and TPM's deflation of every other gene in Root2 — made Root2's whole profile an outlier, so PC1 captured that artefact rather than tissue (1 p).</details>

#### Gene function: co-expression & databases (M4.W1.E4 + D1–D3)

**Q5 (4 p) — Co-expression = guilt by association.** (a) What does a tight co-expression neighbourhood let you infer about your gene, and what does it *not*? (b) Your top neighbour has PCC 0.97. Give **two distinct** explanations that produce this *without* the two genes physically interacting, and say why correlation alone cannot tell "A regulates B" from "a third factor drives both".

<details><summary>✅ Model answer (4 p)</summary>(a) A shared expression pattern is a <b>hypothesis</b> that the genes share a process or regulator (1 p); it is <b>not</b> proof of physical interaction or direct regulation — correlation ≠ causation (1 p). (b) Two of: a shared upstream regulator switches both on; both are specific to the same tissue; both respond independently to the same condition (e.g. stress). Correlation is <b>symmetric and unsigned</b>, so it cannot distinguish "A→B", "B→A" or "C→both" — that needs directed / perturbation evidence (2 p).</details>

**Q6 (4 p) — Specificity of evidence.** Your gene and a transcription factor both peak in the mature stem **and** both localise to the xylem in the root eFP. (a) Why is shared tissue *and* shared cell type stronger evidence of a functional link than shared tissue alone? (b) Give one way two genes could share a tissue yet **not** be functionally related.

<details><summary>✅ Model answer (4 p)</summary>(a) The more <i>specific</i> the shared context, the lower the chance of coincidence — co-localising at cell-type resolution rules out the trivial "both are just stem-abundant" explanation, so the guilt-by-association is stronger (2 p). (b) Housekeeping / broadly high genes are abundant everywhere; or both genes respond independently to the same cue (e.g. both stress-induced) without working together (2 p).</details>

**Q7 (4 p) — Reproducibility across atlases.** Suppose three of your M4.W1.E4 top co-expressed genes also show up in your gene's CoNekT neighbourhood, but one does not. (a) What does cross-atlas reproducibility tell you that a single atlas cannot? (b) Give two distinct reasons a *real* partner could be missing from one atlas's list.

<details><summary>✅ Model answer (4 p)</summary>(a) Recurrence across <i>independent</i> datasets argues the correlation is genuine biology, not a batch/condition artefact of one experiment (2 p). (b) Any two of: different tissues/conditions sampled (the partnership is condition-specific); different normalization / network method / correlation cutoff; the gene is absent from that database's genome version or was filtered out (2 p).</details>

**Q8 (3 p) — Reading a disagreement.** Three databases agree your gene's top organ is stem but rank the 2nd/3rd organs differently. (a) Which disagreement matters more for your conclusion, and why? (b) What property of the underlying data most often explains rank shuffling low down the list?

<details><summary>✅ Model answer (3 p)</summary>(a) The <b>top-organ agreement</b> carries the biological conclusion (where the gene acts); the low-expression rank order sits near the detection floor and is noisy, so reshuffling there is expected and harmless (2 p). (b) Different sample sets / conditions (and sequencing depth / normalization) between atlases (1 p).</details>

> **✍️ Dossier:** keep your answers — the reasoning here (why TPM, artefact vs batch, PCA trust, correlation vs causation, evidence types) is exactly what the conference Q&A and the rubric (criteria 1 & 3) probe.

# Week 2 — uge 44 · gene-regulatory networks

## 📅 Tuesday 28 Oct · 09:50–12:00 {.dayband}

::: {.dayband-sub}
Group work — today you do **M4.W2.E1 → M4.W2.E5** (N0 → N4) on **your own** gene. **E6** (edge types) and the optional **MYB46 appendix** are flex / homework.
:::

### Build & measure your gene's network  *(R, interactive in the browser)*

You build and measure **your own gene's** network, layer by layer: its co-expression neighbourhood (**N1**), a **physical** layer from BioGRID (**N2**), and a **regulatory** layer for your gene from PlantConnectome (**N3**). Then you **measure** it (**N4**) — is your module a clique or a star, and does anything regulate your gene? **N5** spells out what the three edge types do and don't license. *(An optional appendix at the end shows the hand-curated **MYB46 GRN** as a gold-standard example to compare with your own.)*

Each build step (**N1 → N2 → N3**) **draws the network right in the page** — drag nodes, scroll to zoom, and use the **layout buttons** (Spread / Circle / Concentric / Grid / Hierarchy) if it looks crowded — so you watch your gene's network grow layer by layer: co-expression, then physical (PPI), then regulatory.

> **By the end of Week 2 you can:** (1) build and read a co-expression network for *your own* gene; (2) tell co-expression, physical (PPI) and regulatory (GRN) edges apart, and say what each does and doesn't license; (3) find a **hub**, a **bottleneck** (betweenness) and an **articulation point**, and explain why removing MYB46 shatters the cascade; (4) explain why you **cannot** read a regulatory *sign* or *direction* off a correlation.

---

> **How to run today.** Work through **N0 → N4** below as a group — organise yourselves however you like. Everything you produce feeds your **1-page gene dossier** (the 📋 panel, bottom-left), which you **hand in on Thursday**, not today. **N5** (edge types) and the optional **MYB46 appendix** are flex / homework.

### M4.W2.E1 · N0 — (Re)claim your gene

webR forgets everything when the page reloads, so **set your gene here** before the network steps — whether you're continuing from Week 1 or starting a fresh session. Use **the same gene you claimed in M4.W1.E3** (any gene from that pool).

> **Got an "object not found" error later, or reloaded the page?** webR forgets all state on reload — just re-run **N0 → N1 → N2 → N3 → N4** top-to-bottom once, then continue.

```{webr}
MY_GENE <- "______"        # <- the AGI locus CODE, e.g. "AT5G17420"  (must be exact - this is what looks the gene up)
MY_NAME <- lab(MY_GENE)    # the gene's symbol, looked up for you (falls back to the AGI if it has none)

say(grepl("^AT[1-5CM]G[0-9]{5}$", MY_GENE) && MY_GENE %in% rownames(EXPR),
    paste("adopted", MY_NAME, "(", MY_GENE, ") — ready for the network."),
    "pick a gene from the pool above (e.g. MY_GENE <- \"AT5G17420\") and re-run.")
```

### M4.W2.E2 · N1 — Build your co-expression network

webR forgets on reload, so we recompute how strongly **every** gene correlates with yours, then build a network with **one knob**: a correlation **cutoff** that decides *both* which genes are in (all genes correlated with your gene above it) *and* which gene-pairs get an edge. Raise the cutoff → fewer, tighter genes; lower it → more. *(Run N0 first so `MY_GENE` is set.)*

```{webr}
if (!exists("MY_GENE")) stop("Run N0 first to set your gene (MY_GENE).")
HUB    <- MY_GENE                                  # your adopted gene (from N0)
target <- EXPR[HUB, ]                              # its expression across every organ
pcc    <- apply(EXPR, 1, function(r) suppressWarnings(cor(r, target)))  # corr of EVERY gene with yours
pcc[is.na(pcc)] <- 0                               # a flat gene gives NA -> treat as uncorrelated
nbhd   <- data.frame(gene = rownames(EXPR), symbol = lab(rownames(EXPR)),
                     description = substr(desc[rownames(EXPR)], 1, 40), PCC = round(pcc, 3),
                     row.names = NULL)             # row.names = NULL -> the AGI appears ONCE, in the gene column
nbhd   <- nbhd[order(-nbhd$PCC), ]
print(head(nbhd, 12), right = FALSE, row.names = FALSE)   # left-aligned; row 1 = your gene, PCC = 1.000

# guide — how big is the network at each cutoff? (the cutoff alone sets the size — explore it)
for (cut0 in c(0.70, 0.80, 0.85, 0.90, 0.95))
  cat("  cutoff", cut0, "->", sum(pcc >= cut0), "genes\n")

# ONE knob: genes correlated with your gene above the cutoff = the network's nodes (your gene is always in)
MY_CUTOFF <- ______                                # <- e.g. 0.9   (raise -> fewer, tighter; lower -> more genes — explore it)
nb <- head(nbhd$gene[nbhd$PCC >= MY_CUTOFF], 200)  # the cutoff sets the size; 200 is only a browser-safety limit

# draw an edge between any TWO of those genes whose profiles also correlate above the cutoff
C    <- cor(t(EXPR[nb, , drop = FALSE]))            # gene × gene correlation among the selected genes
ut   <- upper.tri(C)                               # each pair once (not the diagonal)
keep <- ut & C > MY_CUTOFF
edges <- data.frame(source = rownames(C)[row(C)[keep]],
                    target = colnames(C)[col(C)[keep]], type = "coexpression")

cat("\nAt cutoff", MY_CUTOFF, "->", length(nb), "genes",
    if (length(nb) >= 200) "(hit the 200 safety limit — raise the cutoff)" else "", "and", nrow(edges), "edges.\n")
cynet(edges, hub = HUB, id = "cy_n1", title = paste(MY_NAME, "co-expression network (cutoff", MY_CUTOFF, ")"))

say(length(nb) > 1 && nrow(edges) > 0,
    paste0("network at cutoff ", MY_CUTOFF, ": ", length(nb), " genes, ", nrow(edges),
           " edges. Raise the cutoff for a tighter core; lower it for a broader module — explore it."),
    "fill MY_CUTOFF (e.g. 0.9). If you get almost nothing, lower it.")
```

> **🔬 One knob, one network.** `MY_CUTOFF` does two jobs at once — it decides which genes are *in* (those correlated with yours) **and** which pairs get an edge. The guide printed above shows how many genes join at each cutoff — **raise** `MY_CUTOFF` and only the most tightly co-expressed genes remain (a small, clean core); **lower** it and the module grows toward a broader neighbourhood. Because these genes are *defined* by being co-expressed with yours, the network stays **densely connected** even at high cutoffs — that density is the hallmark of a real functional module, not a bug. **Drag nodes apart** in the viewer to read it; **start around `0.9` and explore** — a very low cutoff pulls in many genes and makes a large, slow mesh.

### M4.W2.E3 · N2 — Add the physical layer (BioGRID PPI)

Your co-expression edges (N1) say "these genes behave alike." Now overlay **physical** protein–protein interactions from BioGRID — where two neighbours actually *touch*. N2 draws an edge wherever **any two** genes in your neighbourhood interact — not only those touching your gene (so the CESA4/7/8 triangle appears even if your gene is not a CESA). **Many genes have no BioGRID interactions at all** — an empty layer is a real finding. *(Run N1 first so `edges` and `nb` exist.)*

```{webr}
if (!exists("edges") || !exists("nb")) stop("Run N1 first so 'edges' and 'nb' exist.")
edges <- edges[edges$type == "coexpression", , drop = FALSE]   # start fresh from your N1 co-expression edges
# overlay BioGRID physical interactions where BOTH partners are in your neighbourhood
pp <- ppi[ppi$source %in% nb & ppi$target %in% nb, c("source","target")]
if (nrow(pp) > 0) {
  pp  <- pp[pp$source != pp$target, , drop = FALSE]                       # drop self-loops
  key <- apply(pp, 1, function(r) paste(sort(r), collapse = "|"))         # PPI is undirected: one key per pair
  pp  <- pp[!duplicated(key), , drop = FALSE]                             # so A-B and B-A don't draw twice
  if (nrow(pp) > 0) { pp$type <- "PPI"; edges <- rbind(edges, pp) }
}

cesa <- c("AT5G44030","AT5G17420","AT4G18780")     # the secondary-wall CESA triangle
cesa_ppi <- sum(edges$type == "PPI" & edges$source %in% cesa & edges$target %in% cesa)
cat("Edges now:", nrow(edges), " (PPI:", sum(edges$type == "PPI"),
    "; CESA–CESA physical edges:", cesa_ppi, ")\n")

# draw the network so far — Layers 1+2 (blue edges = physical PPI)
cynet(edges, hub = MY_GENE, id = "cy_n2", title = "Layers 1+2: co-expression (grey) + physical PPI (blue)")

say(exists("edges") && nrow(edges) > 0,
    paste0("physical layer done — ", sum(edges$type == "PPI"), " PPI edge(s) among your neighbours. Zero is itself a finding: BioGRID coverage is sparse for many genes (even MYB46 has none). If CESA4/7/8 are here, their PPI triangle appears."),
    "run N1 first so 'edges' and 'nb' exist, then re-run.")
```

### M4.W2.E4 · N3 — Add the regulatory layer  *(PlantConnectome)*

Co-expression (N1) and PPI (N2) are **undirected** — they cannot say who controls whom. Now add the **regulatory** layer from **PlantConnectome** (directed, signed, PubMed-cited edges text-mined from tens of thousands of papers). The cell reports two things: **who regulates your gene** (and what it regulates), and — the strongest signal — **how many regulatory edges fall *between two of your co-expressed genes*** (co-expression **and** regulation on the same pair is the best convergence you can show). **Many genes have none** (housekeeping genes, or genes the literature hasn't resolved) — an empty layer is a real finding, not a failure. *(Run N1 first so `nb` exists.)*

```{webr}
if (!exists("nb")) stop("Run N1 first so 'nb' (your neighbourhood) exists.")
rg     <- connectome_grn[connectome_grn$source_AGI %in% nb | connectome_grn$target_AGI %in% nb, ]  # edges touching your module
within <- rg[rg$source_AGI %in% nb & rg$target_AGI %in% nb, ]      # BOTH ends co-expressed -> regulation AMONG your module
my_regs <- unique(rg$source_AGI[rg$target_AGI == MY_GENE])         # who regulates your gene
my_tgts <- unique(rg$target_AGI[rg$source_AGI == MY_GENE])         # what your gene regulates
if (nrow(rg) == 0) {
  cat(sprintf("PlantConnectome has no regulatory edges touching %s's module.\n", MY_NAME))
  cat("Common for housekeeping genes (ribosomes, histones) or genes the literature hasn't resolved — the absence is a finding.\n")
} else {
  cat(sprintf("%s: %d regulator(s) in, %d target(s) out.\n", MY_NAME, length(my_regs), length(my_tgts)))
  cat(sprintf("%d regulatory edges touch your module; %d of them are BETWEEN two of your co-expressed genes\n", nrow(rg), nrow(within)))
  cat("  -> co-expression AND regulation on the same pair = the strongest convergence you can show.\n")
  pri   <- rbind(within, rg[rg$source_AGI == MY_GENE | rg$target_AGI == MY_GENE, ], rg)   # draw the interesting edges first
  pri   <- pri[!duplicated(paste(pri$source_AGI, pri$target_AGI)), ]
  drawn <- head(pri, 70)                                            # cap the drawing so it stays readable
  reg_edges <- data.frame(source = drawn$source_AGI, target = drawn$target_AGI, type = drawn$type)
  cynet(reg_edges, hub = MY_GENE, id = "cy_n3",
        title = paste(MY_NAME, "regulation — green activates, red represses, grey regulates;",
                      if (nrow(rg) > 70) paste("top 70 of", nrow(rg)) else "PlantConnectome"))
  say(TRUE, sprintf("%d regulatory edge(s) around your module, %d of them among co-expressed genes — directed, signed, PubMed-cited (unlike co-expression, N1).", nrow(rg), nrow(within)), "-")
}
```

> **Text-mined = a lead, not proof.** PlantConnectome is read from sentences by an LLM, so treat one edge as a hypothesis to verify; the strong signal is **convergence** (a regulatory edge that is *also* a co-expression or PPI edge). You'll meet a hand-curated, experiment-typed gold-standard network in the **optional MYB46 appendix**.

### M4.W2.E5 · N4 — Measure YOUR gene's network

Put numbers on **your own** module. The base-R helpers below (`build_adj`, `betweenness_base`, `clustering_matrix` — black boxes, just call them) answer: is your **co-expression module** (N1) a tight **clique** or a loose **star**, and which neighbour is its **secondary bridge**? The cell then **plots your network with the metrics on it** (node size = degree, fill = betweenness). And from N3: is your gene a **target** (regulated), a **regulator**, or a **leaf**?

> **🔑 Vocabulary:** **degree** = edges at a node · **hub** = high-degree node · **betweenness** = how many shortest paths pass *through* a node (a *bottleneck*) · **clustering** = do my neighbours link to *each other*? (≈1 clique, ≈0 star).

```{webr}
if (!exists("edges") || !exists("nb") || !exists("MY_GENE")) stop("Run N0, N1, N2 first.")

# ---- base-R network helpers (no packages) — black boxes: call and read the result ----
build_adj <- function(edges, directed = FALSE) {
  nodes <- sort(unique(c(edges$source, edges$target)))
  A <- matrix(0L, length(nodes), length(nodes), dimnames = list(nodes, nodes))
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(edges))) { A[edges$source[i], edges$target[i]] <- 1L
    if (!directed) A[edges$target[i], edges$source[i]] <- 1L }
  diag(A) <- 0L; A
}
betweenness_base <- function(A) {               # Brandes' algorithm (unweighted)
  nm <- rownames(A); n <- length(nm); CB <- setNames(numeric(n), nm)
  for (s in nm) {
    S <- character(0); P <- setNames(vector("list", n), nm)
    sigma <- setNames(rep(0, n), nm); sigma[s] <- 1
    d <- setNames(rep(-1, n), nm); d[s] <- 0; q <- s
    while (length(q) > 0) { v <- q[1]; q <- q[-1]; S <- c(S, v)
      for (w in nm[A[v, ] == 1L]) {
        if (d[w] < 0) { d[w] <- d[v] + 1; q <- c(q, w) }
        if (d[w] == d[v] + 1) { sigma[w] <- sigma[w] + sigma[v]; P[[w]] <- c(P[[w]], v) } } }
    delta <- setNames(rep(0, n), nm)
    for (w in rev(S)) { for (v in P[[w]]) delta[v] <- delta[v] + (sigma[v]/sigma[w]) * (1 + delta[w])
      if (w != s) CB[w] <- CB[w] + delta[w] } }
  CB / 2
}
clustering_matrix <- function(A) {
  k <- rowSums(A); tri <- diag(A %*% (A %*% A)) / 2; denom <- k * (k - 1) / 2
  ifelse(denom > 0, tri / denom, 0)
}
components_base <- function(A) {
  nm <- rownames(A); comp <- setNames(rep(NA_integer_, length(nm)), nm); k <- 0
  for (start in nm) if (is.na(comp[start])) { k <- k + 1; q <- start; comp[start] <- k
    while (length(q) > 0) { u <- q[1]; q <- q[-1]
      for (w in nm[A[u, ] == 1L]) if (is.na(comp[w])) { comp[w] <- k; q <- c(q, w) } } }
  comp
}

# ---- your CO-EXPRESSION module: clique or star, hub/bridge, drawn with metrics on it ----
co <- edges[edges$type == "coexpression", c("source","target"), drop = FALSE]
nn <- length(unique(c(co$source, co$target)))
if (nn > 2 && MY_GENE %in% c(co$source, co$target)) {
  As <- build_adj(co); deg <- rowSums(As); cc_own <- clustering_matrix(As)
  mean_ncc <- mean(cc_own[names(cc_own) != MY_GENE])
  cat(sprintf("Co-expression module: %d genes, %d edges. Mean neighbour clustering = %.2f -> %s.\n",
              nn, nrow(co), mean_ncc, if (mean_ncc >= 0.5) "a tight CLIQUE (a coherent unit)" else "a looser STAR"))
  if (nn <= 80) {
    btw <- betweenness_base(As); others <- btw[names(btw) != MY_GENE]
    if (length(others) && max(others) > 0)
      cat(sprintf("Secondary bridge: %s (betweenness %.1f) — the neighbour the others most pass through.\n",
                  lab(names(which.max(others))), max(others)))
    else cat("No secondary bridge — a near-pure star; the neighbours barely interconnect.\n")
    nrm  <- function(v) if (diff(range(v)) > 0) (v - min(v)) / diff(range(v)) else rep(.5, length(v))
    heat <- colorRampPalette(c("#f7f7f7","#fdae6b","#e6550d","#a50f15"))(24)
    g <- names(deg)
    cynet(co, hub = MY_GENE, id = "cy_n4",
          title = paste(MY_NAME, "network — node size: degree | fill: betweenness (reddest = bottleneck)"),
          node_fill = setNames(heat[1 + round(nrm(btw[g]) * 23)], g),
          node_size = setNames(24 + 34 * nrm(deg[g]), g))
  } else cat("Module >80 genes — raise MY_CUTOFF in N1 for a crisper core to measure the bridge and plot the metrics.\n")
} else cat("Co-expression module too small — lower MY_CUTOFF in N1 and re-run.\n")

# ---- your REGULATORY position (from N3). Most genes are TARGETS or LEAVES — only TFs are masters ----
if (exists("my_regs")) {
  ni <- length(my_regs); no <- length(my_tgts)
  role <- if (ni + no == 0) "a LEAF — nothing in your module is a documented regulator of it (usual for a non-TF gene)" else
          if (no > 0)       "a REGULATOR — your gene appears to control others in the module (it may be a TF)" else
                            "a TARGET — your gene is regulated by others in the module"
  cat(sprintf("Regulatory position: %d regulator(s) in, %d target(s) out -> %s.\n", ni, no, role))
} else cat("Run N3 to read your regulatory position.\n")

say(nn > 2, "measured YOUR network — its shape (clique/star), hub/bridge, and your gene's regulatory role. These go straight into your dossier; every gene is different.",
    "run N1 (and N3) first, then re-run.")
```

> **Into your dossier:** your module's shape (clique vs star), its secondary bridge, and your gene's regulatory role (usually **target** or **leaf** — most genes are regulated, not regulators). Every gene gives a different answer — that is your result to present.

### M4.W2.E6 · N5 — What the three edge types mean

An edge isn't just a line — its meaning is fixed by **what it represents, whether it's directed, and what experiment made it**. Only the regulatory layer licenses a knockout prediction.

| | **Co-expression** | **PPI (BioGRID)** | **GRN (regulatory)** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Edge means | mRNA levels co-vary | proteins physically interact | a TF controls a target's transcription |
| Directed? | **No** | **No** | **Yes** (TF → target) |
| Sign | ± correlation | none | + activates / − represses |
| Predict a knockout? | no (correlative) | no (physical) | **yes** (a testable causal prediction) |
| Confirmed by | RNA-seq correlation | Y2H, AP-MS | ChIP, EMSA, transactivation |

Causal ranking: **GRN > PPI > co-expression** — *co-expression finds candidates, PPI shows partnerships, GRN gives the most direct evidence of control.* (Even then a GRN edge only *licenses* a knockout hypothesis — **redundancy** can mask the phenotype.) Two paradoxes from the data: **(1)** MYB46 *regulates* CESA7 but has **zero PPI edges** (in BioGRID) — a TF binds its target's DNA, not its protein — so the absence is informative, not a gap. **(2)** CESA4/7/8 are linked in **all three** layers (co-expression + PPI triangle + shared MYB46 regulator) — three independent assays converging is far stronger than any one edge.

> **✍️ For your dossier — your network vs the gold standard.** Name **one** structural feature *your* co-expression module (N1 / N4) has that the MYB46 cascade lacks, and **one** the cascade has that yours lacks. *(Think: undirected vs directed, unsigned vs signed, dense clique vs sparse star — and what happens when you delete the single most central node: your module degrades gradually, the cascade shatters the moment MYB46 goes.)*

### Close the dossier

*(Functional enrichment is an optional extension — see the **Appendix** at the end of this page.)*

**✍️ Dossier (assessed) — close it out (about *your* gene):**

1. **What & where:** your gene's molecular identity (its Pfam domain) and where it acts — its top organ plus the finest cell type / tissue you could find, from eFP / PEO.
2. **Its module:** your top co-expressed genes and the **process** they name. Does it match your M4.W1.E3 hypothesis?
3. **Cross-check:** do the databases (eFP / PEO / CoNekT / EBI) **agree** on your gene's tissue, partners and domain?
4. **Correlation vs regulation** *(from the MYB46 case study)*: why is co-expression **not** proof that one gene regulates another? Use the MYB46→CESA / KNAT7 ⊣ CESA8 example.
5. **Verdict:** does the evidence **confirm or revise** your hypothesis? Name **≥3** evidence types — any three of: expression pattern, a co-expression neighbour, a database hit, a PPI / regulatory edge, and (*only if you ran the Appendix*) an enriched GO term.

**📄 Assemble your 1-page dossier (the conference hand-in).** Fill these in the **📋 Dossier** panel (bottom-left) as you go — it autosaves, you can **Download** it, and **Check with AI** gives formative feedback. Transfer them onto one page, in order (template: `Module4_GeneDossier_and_Rubric`):

1. **Data quality** (M4.W1.E2) — one line: the `Gene8` artefact you detected and removed, and why.
2. **Hypothesis** (M4.W1.E3) — your adopted gene + your one-line guess at its function.
3. **Co-expression** (M4.W1.E4) — your top-5 neighbours + the module they name.
4. **Database cross-check** (M4.W1.E5 · D1–D3) — your filled results table.
5. **Network** (M4.W2 · N1–N5) — a screenshot of *your gene's* network **and one metric you measured on it in N4** (its clique-vs-star clustering, its secondary bridge, or your regulatory role), plus (optionally) one insight from the **MYB46 appendix example** (the hub / the KNAT7 ⊣ CESA8 brake).
6. **Verdict** (M4.W2) — confirm or revise, naming ≥3 evidence types.

> **Graded (5 criteria):** data quality & normalization reasoning (15%) · **your gene's expression + co-expression** characterisation (30%) · **database cross-check (20%)** · interpretation — correlation-vs-regulation + a verdict with named evidence (20%) · communication & Q&A (15%). You present this at the **student conference** (~5-min group talk).

### 📝 Week 2 — exam-style questions  *(assessed; 2025-exam style, point-scored)*

The network half of the exam. Answer in 2–4 sentences; points match the grading. *(A larger 18-question bank exists in the teacher materials; these seven are the core.)* These questions probe the **shared** MYB46 GRN — the concepts transfer to any gene; your **own** gene is assessed in the dossier.

**W2·Q1 (4 p) — Read the hub.** In the MYB46 GRN, MYB46 has the highest **out-degree**, the highest **betweenness**, and a **near-zero clustering coefficient**. Interpret each metric biologically, then say what network position they describe together.

<details><summary>✅ Model answer (4 p)</summary>High out-degree = it directly regulates many targets (master switch); high betweenness = most shortest paths run through it (a bottleneck — NAC signals reach the biosynthesis genes only via MYB46); near-zero clustering = its targets don't connect to each other (a <b>star</b>, not a clique) (3 p, 1 each). Together: a central <b>hub / bottleneck</b> the whole cascade is funnelled through (1 p).</details>

**W2·Q2 (4 p) — Same degree, different role.** SND1, CESA8 and KNAT7 all have **degree 3**, yet their betweenness is 8.0 / 8.0 / 0.3 and their clustering coefficient 0.33 / 0.33 / 0.67. (a) How can three nodes of *equal degree* differ so much in betweenness and clustering? (b) What do KNAT7's high clustering + near-zero betweenness tell you about its position, and would removing it fragment the network?

<details><summary>✅ Model answer (4 p)</summary>(a) Degree counts only a node's immediate links; <b>betweenness</b> depends on whether it lies on shortest paths *between other* nodes (a bridge), and <b>clustering</b> on whether its own neighbours interlink — both are about global position, not local count (2 p). (b) KNAT7 sits inside a triangle (its neighbours connect to each other → high clustering) and on no unique shortest path (→ ~0 betweenness): it is <b>embedded/peripheral</b>, not a bottleneck, so removing it leaves the network connected (1 component) (2 p).</details>

**W2·Q3 (4 p) — Name the motif.** MYB46 activates **both** CESA8 and KNAT7, and KNAT7 represses CESA8. (a) Name this motif. (b) Why is it *not* negative feedback, and what behaviour does it produce?

<details><summary>✅ Model answer (4 p)</summary>(a) An <b>incoherent feed-forward loop</b> (type-1 IFFL) (2 p). (b) It is feed-<i>forward</i>, not feedback: MYB46 sits upstream of both arms and KNAT7 never acts back on MYB46. It gives a <b>self-limiting / pulse-like</b> activation of CESA8 — a built-in brake that sharpens the response rather than a sustained on/off loop (2 p).</details>

**W2·Q4 (4 p) — Robustness.** Deleting MYB46 *in silico* splits the network into 13 components; deleting a single CESA barely changes it. (a) What does this say about each node's role and the network's fragility? (b) What is the one-word graph term for a node like MYB46?

<details><summary>✅ Model answer (4 p)</summary>(a) MYB46 holds the cascade together — losing it <b>fragments</b> the network (high lethality-centrality; the architecture is fragile to losing this one hub), whereas a peripheral CESA loses only its own few edges, leaving the rest connected (robust) (3 p). (b) An <b>articulation point</b> (cut vertex) (1 p).</details>

**W2·Q5 (4 p) — A repressor that co-expresses *positively*.** KNAT7 **represses** CESA8, yet across the atlas KNAT7 and CESA8 are *positively* co-expressed (both rise in secondary-wall tissue). (a) How can a repressor positively correlate with its own target? (b) What does this prove about inferring a regulatory *sign* from co-expression?

<details><summary>✅ Model answer (4 p)</summary>(a) Both are switched on by the same upstream master, MYB46 (which activates KNAT7 *and* CESA8) — the shared driver makes them rise together across tissues, and that correlation dominates over KNAT7's direct repressive effect (the incoherent feed-forward structure — see the MYB46 appendix) (2 p). (b) Co-expression **sign and direction carry no regulatory meaning**: a positive correlation can hide a repression, and you cannot read activation/repression or who-regulates-whom off a correlation — only directed, signed (GRN/perturbation) evidence can (2 p).</details>

**W2·Q6 (5 p) — Physical vs regulatory edges.** In your network CESA4/7/8 are joined by **BioGRID PPI** edges (N2), but MYB46 reaches its targets only through the **curated GRN** (the MYB46 appendix) — never by a PPI edge. (a) Mechanistically, why does a TF have **no** physical-interaction edge to the genes it controls? (b) What experiment type draws the MYB46→CESA edge instead? (c) What general rule about reading a single edge type follows?

<details><summary>✅ Model answer (5 p)</summary>(a) A TF binds its target gene's <b>promoter DNA</b>, not the target's protein; PPI assays (Y2H, AP-MS) detect protein–protein contact, so a regulatory TF→target link is invisible to them (2 p). (b) A curated <b>GRN</b> edge from ChIP-seq / EMSA / transactivation, showing MYB46 binds the SMRE/M46RE elements in the CESA promoters (2 p). (c) Each edge type carries only <b>one</b> kind of evidence; the absence of a PPI edge is not absence of a relationship — read which layer an edge comes from and combine them (1 p).</details>

**W2·Q7 (4 p) — Synthesis (your gene).** (a) In one sentence, state your gene's function and name **three independent evidence types** from your dossier that support it. (b) Which of those is the **weakest** for *proving* the function, and why?

<details><summary>✅ Model answer (4 p)</summary>(a) One defensible claim + three correctly-typed evidence lines — e.g. <i>"CESA7 is a secondary-wall cellulose synthase acting in stem xylem"</i>: <b>expression</b> (stem/xylem peak across ePlant + PEO + EBI), <b>co-expression</b> (the CESA4/8 module reproduced in your atlas + CoNekT), <b>physical / regulatory</b> (the CESA PPI triangle in N2 + a MYB46→CESA regulatory edge in N3) — 3 p, 1 per correctly-typed type. (b) <b>Co-expression is weakest</b> — it is only correlation (guilt by association), consistent with but not proof; a physical (BioGRID PPI) or ChIP/EMSA-backed regulatory edge is far stronger (1 p).</details>

> **✍️ Dossier:** these seven are exactly what the conference panel asks — bring named evidence (a metric, an experiment, a reference) to each answer.
